name: Foot and ankle bones (right)
description: Right foot skeleton: 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals and 14 phalanges, with the distal tibia and fibula for context.

source.attribution: BodyParts3D, (c) The Database Center for Life Science, licensed under CC Attribution-Share Alike 2.1 Japan
source.anatomy_verified: Geometry and identity taken from BodyParts3D (FMA IDs preserved). Shapes simplified for the web only.
source.conversion_notes: Binary STL converted to GLB: vertices welded, meshes simplified with quadric decimation for web delivery, smooth normals, axes converted to Y-up/Z-anterior, recentred, one node per structure. Structures marked "merged" are the union of several BodyParts3D meshes (e.g. the parts of one muscle); structures with a "component" take one connected part of a BodyParts3D mesh, chosen by position.

groups.label: Foot and ankle
groups.tip: Your foot has 26 bones: seven tarsals, five metatarsals and 14 phalanges. They form springy arches that spread your weight with every step.

groups.label: Leg (distal)
groups.tip: The ankle bumps are the malleoli. The inner one belongs to the tibia, and the outer one, a little lower, belongs to the fibula.

groups.label: Tarsal bones
groups.tip: Tiger Cubs Need MILC names the tarsals: talus, calcaneus, navicular, the medial, intermediate and lateral cuneiforms, and cuboid.

groups.label: Metatarsals
groups.tip: The metatarsals are numbered one to five, starting at the big toe. Their rounded heads make the ball of your foot.

groups.label: Phalanges of the toes
groups.tip: Each smaller toe has three phalanges, but the big toe has only two. That makes 14 in all, just like your hand.

content.origin: From the Latin word for shin bone. The word also meant a flute, because early flutes were made from animal shin bones.
content.location: It is the big bone on the inner side of your lower leg. This model shows only its lower end, sitting on top of the talus.
content.description: Its lower end is wide and smooth underneath. On the inner side it juts down into the medial malleolus, the bump on the inside of your ankle.
content.function: It carries your body weight from the knee down to the foot. It forms the roof and the inner wall of your ankle joint.
content.mnemonic: Tibia is the Thick one. It sits on the inside, on the big toe side.
content.clinical: A bad twist of the ankle can snap off its inner bump, the medial malleolus.
content.hint: Look for the thick leg bone that ends in the bump on the inside of the ankle.

content.origin: From the Latin word for a brooch pin or clasp. It is thin, like the pin of a brooch.
content.location: It is the thin bone on the outer side of your lower leg. This model shows only its lower end, beside the tibia and talus.
content.description: A slim bone whose lower end forms the lateral malleolus, the bump on the outside of your ankle.
content.function: It forms the outer wall of your ankle joint and stops the talus sliding sideways. Ankle ligaments and leg muscles attach to it.
content.mnemonic: FibuLa is Lateral and Little. Two L words for the thin outer bone.
content.clinical: In the common rolled ankle, the ligaments that tear run from this bone's lower end to the talus and heel bone.
content.hint: Look for the thin leg bone that ends in the bump on the outside of the ankle.

content.origin: From the Latin word for ankle bone. Long ago, people used animal ankle bones as dice.
content.location: It is the top bone of the foot. It sits between the tibia and fibula above and the heel bone below.
content.description: It has a head, a neck and a body. Its top is a smooth pulley that fits between your two ankle bumps, and no muscles attach to it at all.
content.function: It passes your weight from the leg to the foot. Above, it makes the up and down ankle joint, and below, the joint that tilts your sole in and out.
content.mnemonic: Tiger Cubs Need MILC names the tarsal bones. T is for Talus, the one on Top.
content.clinical: A break through its neck can cut off the blood supply to the rest of the bone. Starved of blood, that part may die, which is called avascular necrosis.
content.hint: Find the top foot bone that locks in between the two ankle bumps, with no muscles attached.

questions.text: Which foot bone meets the tibia and fibula to form the ankle joint?
questions.explanation: The talus sits snugly between the tibia and fibula. It is the only foot bone in the ankle joint.

questions.text: Why is a break through the neck of the talus a worry?
options: It always damages the Achilles tendon
The body of the talus can lose its blood supply
It stops the toes from bending
questions.explanation: Blood vessels reach the talus through its neck. A break there can starve the body of blood, so that part of the bone may die.

content.origin: From the Latin word calx, meaning heel. The same word also meant chalk or limestone.
content.location: It is your heel bone, at the back and bottom of the foot, below the talus and behind the cuboid.
content.description: The biggest tarsal bone. Its back end forms your heel, and a shelf on its inner side holds up the talus like a bracket.
content.function: It takes your weight as your heel hits the ground. Your calf muscles pull on it through the Achilles tendon to point your foot, as when you stand on tiptoe.
content.mnemonic: Tiger Cubs Need MILC. The first C is for Calcaneus, the chunky heel.
content.clinical: Plantar fasciitis causes heel pain where a tough band under the foot attaches to this bone. Landing on your feet from a height can shatter it.
content.hint: Find the biggest tarsal bone, forming the heel where the Achilles tendon attaches.

questions.text: Which tendon attaches to the back of the heel bone?
questions.explanation: Your calf muscles pull on the back of the calcaneus through the Achilles tendon, also called the calcaneal tendon.

questions.text: What is the largest tarsal bone?
questions.explanation: The calcaneus, your heel bone, is the largest tarsal bone.

content.origin: From the Latin for little boat. It is shaped like a small boat.
content.location: It sits on the inner side of the foot, between the head of the talus behind and the three wedge-shaped cuneiforms in front.
content.description: A boat-shaped bone, hollow at the back for the talus. On its inner side is a bump you can feel just in front of and below your inner ankle bump.
content.function: It is the keystone of the arch on the inner side of your foot. The main tendon of tibialis posterior grips its bump and helps hold the arch up.
content.mnemonic: Tiger Cubs Need MILC. N is for Navicular, a little boat floating at the top of your arch.
content.clinical: Runners and jumpers can get stress fractures here, and they are easy to miss. Some people have an extra bone beside it that can be painful.
content.hint: Find the boat-shaped bone on the inner side of the foot, in front of the talus and behind the three wedge bones.

questions.text: Which bones meet the front of the navicular?
questions.explanation: The front of the navicular has three smooth spots, one for each of the three wedge-shaped cuneiforms.

questions.text: Which muscle's main tendon attaches to the bump on the navicular?
questions.explanation: Tibialis posterior attaches mainly to the navicular's bump. Its pull helps hold up the arch on the inner side of the foot.

content.origin: From the Greek for cube-like. It is roughly the shape of a dice.
content.location: It sits on the outer, little toe side of the foot, between the heel bone behind and the fourth and fifth metatarsals in front.
content.description: A roughly cube-shaped bone. Underneath, it has a groove for the tendon of a leg muscle, fibularis longus.
content.function: It supports the outer arch of the foot and passes load from the last two metatarsals to the heel bone. Its groove works like a pulley for the fibularis longus tendon.
content.mnemonic: Tiger Cubs Need MILC. The last C is for Cuboid, the cube on the outside.
content.clinical: Cuboid syndrome is pain on the outer side of the foot, thought to come from this bone shifting slightly, sometimes after an ankle sprain.
content.hint: Find the cube-shaped tarsal on the little toe side, between the heel bone and the last two metatarsals.

questions.text: Which tarsal bone lies between the heel bone and the fourth and fifth metatarsals?
questions.explanation: The cuboid sits on the outer side of the foot, in front of the heel bone and behind metatarsals four and five.

questions.text: The groove under the cuboid carries which tendon?
questions.explanation: The fibularis longus tendon, also called peroneus longus, runs through the groove under the cuboid like a rope over a pulley.

content.origin: From the Latin for wedge-shaped. Medial means closer to the middle of the body.
content.location: It sits on the inner, big toe side of the foot, between the navicular behind and the first metatarsal in front.
content.description: The biggest of the three wedge bones. Unlike the other two, its wide edge faces down towards the sole.
content.function: It helps build the arch on the inner side of your foot. Two leg muscles, tibialis anterior and fibularis longus, attach here to help hold that arch.
content.mnemonic: Tiger Cubs Need MILC. M is for Medial, the biggest wedge, sitting behind the big toe.
content.clinical: It lies along the Lisfranc joint line, where the midfoot meets the long foot bones. A twist or a crush can injure this line.
content.hint: Find the biggest of the three wedge bones, lined up behind the big toe.

questions.text: The medial cuneiform meets which bone in front?
questions.explanation: The medial cuneiform sits directly behind the first metatarsal, the long bone of the big toe.

content.origin: From the Latin for wedge-shaped. Intermediate means in between.
content.location: It sits between the other two wedge bones, in front of the navicular and behind the second metatarsal.
content.description: The smallest wedge, with its wide edge facing up. It is shorter than its neighbours, leaving a notch where the second metatarsal slots in.
content.function: It helps form the arch across your foot. The notch it leaves locks the second metatarsal in place, keeping the midfoot steady.
content.mnemonic: Tiger Cubs Need MILC. I is for Intermediate, the little wedge In the middle.
content.clinical: Because it helps lock in the second metatarsal, it is often part of Lisfranc injuries of the midfoot.
content.hint: Find the smallest of the three wedge bones, in the middle, right behind the second metatarsal.

questions.text: Which is the smallest cuneiform?
questions.explanation: The intermediate cuneiform, the middle wedge, is the smallest of the three.

content.origin: From the Latin for wedge-shaped. Lateral means towards the outer side.
content.location: It is the outermost wedge bone, between the intermediate cuneiform and the cuboid, and behind the third metatarsal.
content.description: A wedge-shaped bone with its wide edge facing up. In size, it sits between the other two wedges.
content.function: It helps form the arch across the foot. It carries load from the third metatarsal, and parts of the second and fourth, back to the navicular.
content.mnemonic: Tiger Cubs Need MILC. L is for Lateral, the wedge that leans against the cuboid.
content.clinical: It rarely breaks on its own. It is usually hurt along with its neighbours in a Lisfranc injury of the midfoot.
content.hint: Find the outermost wedge bone, touching the cube-shaped tarsal and lined up behind the third toe.

questions.text: Which tarsal bone lies right beside the lateral cuneiform, on its outer side?
questions.explanation: The lateral cuneiform leans against the cuboid on its outer side.

content.origin: From the Greek for beyond the tarsus. These are the long bones just past the ankle and midfoot bones.
content.location: It is the innermost long bone of the foot, running from the medial cuneiform to the big toe.
content.description: The shortest and thickest metatarsal. Two tiny pea-like bones, called sesamoids, sit under its head inside a tendon.
content.function: It carries more weight than any other metatarsal, especially when you push off to walk or run. Tibialis anterior and fibularis longus attach to its base.
content.mnemonic: Count from the big toe: this is number one, the short, thick one. The heads of these bones make the ball of your foot.
content.clinical: A bunion forms when the big toe drifts outward and the head of this bone sticks out. Gout often strikes the joint at its head first.
content.hint: Find the short, thick bone in the ball of the foot, lined up behind the big toe.

questions.text: A bunion is a bump at the head of which bone?
options: Tip bone of the big toe
questions.explanation: In a bunion, or hallux valgus, the big toe drifts outward and the head of the first metatarsal sticks out on the inner side.

questions.text: Which metatarsal is the shortest and thickest?
questions.explanation: The first metatarsal, behind the big toe, is the shortest and thickest.

content.origin: From the Greek for beyond the tarsus. It is the second of the five long bones of the foot.
content.location: It sits behind the second toe. Its base slots into a notch between the medial and lateral cuneiforms.
content.description: Usually the longest metatarsal, with a slim shaft, like a long, thin pole.
content.function: Its locked-in base makes it the steadiest metatarsal. It is the keystone of the midfoot joints and of the arch across the foot.
content.mnemonic: Count from the big toe: number two is the long one, locked in place like a key in a lock.
content.clinical: It is the most common place for a stress fracture, or march fracture, seen in soldiers, runners and after a sudden jump in walking. Its base is central to Lisfranc injuries.
content.hint: Find the longest bone of the forefoot, lined up with the toe next to the big toe.

questions.text: Which metatarsal most often gets a stress fracture, also called a march fracture?
questions.explanation: The long, slim, locked-in second metatarsal takes a lot of repeated stress, so march fractures happen here most.

questions.text: The base of the second metatarsal slots between which bones?
options: The first and third metatarsal heads
questions.explanation: The short middle wedge leaves a notch between the medial and lateral cuneiforms, and the second metatarsal locks into it.

content.origin: From the Greek for beyond the tarsus. It is the middle of the five long foot bones.
content.location: It sits in the middle of the forefoot, between the lateral cuneiform and the third toe.
content.description: A long, straight bone with a base, a shaft and a rounded head. It is a little shorter than its neighbour, the second metatarsal.
content.function: It carries weight across the middle of the forefoot and helps shape the arch that runs across your foot.
content.mnemonic: Count from the big toe: number three is right in the middle of the five.
content.clinical: After the second, it is a common place for stress fractures. Morton's neuroma, a painful thickened nerve, most often sits between its head and the fourth.
content.hint: Find the middle bone of the five in the forefoot, lined up behind the middle toe.

questions.text: Which tarsal bone does the third metatarsal meet?
questions.explanation: The base of the third metatarsal rests against the lateral cuneiform, the outermost wedge bone.

content.origin: From the Greek for beyond the tarsus. It is the fourth of the five long foot bones.
content.location: It sits between the third and fifth metatarsals, running from the cuboid to the fourth toe. It also touches the lateral cuneiform.
content.description: A long bone with a base, shaft and head, a little shorter than the third.
content.function: It supports the outer side of the forefoot. Its joint with the cuboid moves more than the inner ones, helping your foot adjust to bumpy ground.
content.mnemonic: Count from the big toe: numbers four and five both sit on the cuboid, like two friends sharing a seat.
content.clinical: Morton's neuroma is a thickened, painful nerve, most often between the heads of the third and fourth metatarsals. It can feel like a burning pebble in your shoe.
content.hint: Find the forefoot bone behind the second-smallest toe, sitting on the cube-shaped tarsal.

questions.text: Morton's neuroma most often lies between the heads of which metatarsals?
questions.explanation: Morton's neuroma most often affects the nerve that runs between the heads of the third and fourth metatarsals.

content.origin: From the Greek for beyond the tarsus. It is the last of the five, on the outer edge.
content.location: It is the outermost metatarsal, along the outer edge of your foot between the cuboid and the little toe.
content.description: Its base has a big bump on the outer side. You can feel it halfway along the outside edge of your foot.
content.function: It supports the outer edge of the foot. A leg muscle, fibularis brevis, pulls on its bump to turn your sole outward.
content.mnemonic: Count from the big toe: number five is the one with the bump on the outside edge.
content.clinical: Rolling your ankle inward can tear that bump right off, an avulsion fracture. A Jones fracture, a little further along, heals slowly because of a poor blood supply.
content.hint: Find the forefoot bone along the outer edge, with a bony bump at its base halfway along the side of the foot.

questions.text: Which muscle attaches to the bump at the base of the fifth metatarsal?
questions.explanation: Fibularis brevis, also called peroneus brevis, attaches to the bump at the base of the fifth metatarsal.

questions.text: Rolling your ankle inward can pull a chip off the base of which bone?
questions.explanation: When the foot rolls in, fibularis brevis can yank its bump off the base of the fifth metatarsal.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers, because toe bones line up in rows. Hallux is Latin for the big toe.
content.location: It is the first bone of the big toe, just in front of the head of the first metatarsal.
content.description: A short, thick bone, bigger than the first bones of the other toes. The big toe has only two bones.
content.function: It forms the big toe joint, which bends up as your foot pushes off. The small muscles of the big toe attach to its base.
content.mnemonic: The big toe is like your thumb: two bones, near and far, with no middle one.
content.clinical: Turf toe is a sprain of the big toe joint from being bent up too far. Hallux rigidus is arthritis here that makes pushing off stiff and sore.
content.hint: Find the big toe bone sitting just in front of the ball of the foot.

questions.text: How many phalanges, or toe bones, does the big toe have?
questions.explanation: The big toe has two phalanges, proximal and distal, and no middle one, just like your thumb.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. Each small toe has three bones in a row.
content.location: It is the first bone of the second toe, just in front of the head of the second metatarsal.
content.description: A long, slim bone. The second toe is often your longest toe.
content.function: It forms the toe's joint at the ball of the foot, letting the toe bend up as you push off and press down to grip. Small muscles of the sole work across this joint.
content.mnemonic: Proximal means closest, so it is the toe bone closest to your foot. Small toes have three bones each.
content.clinical: Hammer toe is a fixed bend at the joint just beyond this bone. It most often affects the second toe.
content.hint: Find the second toe bone closest to the ball of the foot.

questions.text: Hammer toe is a fixed bend at which joint?
options: Between the proximal and middle phalanges
Between the first metatarsal and medial cuneiform
questions.explanation: In hammer toe, the joint between the proximal and middle phalanges stays bent, so the toe curls like a hammer.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. The third toe's bones line up three in a row.
content.location: It is the first bone of the third toe, just in front of the head of the third metatarsal.
content.description: A slim bone with a cupped base that fits over the round head of the third metatarsal.
content.function: It forms the joint at the ball of the foot, so the toe can bend up as you step off and grip the floor.
content.mnemonic: Proximal means closest to the foot. Three small bones, and this is the first.
content.clinical: Stubbing your toe often breaks a small toe bone like this one. It is usually treated by taping it to the next toe, called buddy strapping.
content.hint: Find the third toe bone closest to the ball of the foot.

questions.text: At its base, the proximal phalanx of the third toe meets which bone?
options: Middle phalanx of the third toe
questions.explanation: At its base, it meets the head of the third metatarsal, at the toe joint in the ball of the foot.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. The fourth toe has its own row of three.
content.location: It is the first bone of the fourth toe, just in front of the head of the fourth metatarsal.
content.description: A slim bone, shorter than those of the second and third toes, with a cupped base for the metatarsal head.
content.function: It forms the joint at the ball of the foot, letting the toe lift as you push off and press down to grip.
content.mnemonic: Proximal means closest to the foot. Each small toe has three bones, and this is the first.
content.clinical: In claw toe, the joint at this bone's base bends up while the joints beyond bend down. It often affects several toes and can come with nerve or muscle disease.
content.hint: Find the fourth toe bone closest to the ball of the foot.

questions.text: Where is the proximal phalanx of the fourth toe?
options: At the tip of the fourth toe
Between the cuboid and the fourth metatarsal
Just past the head of the fourth metatarsal
questions.explanation: The proximal phalanx is the first toe bone, just past the head of its metatarsal.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. The little toe's row starts here.
content.location: It is the first bone of the little toe, just in front of the head of the fifth metatarsal.
content.description: The shortest of the first toe bones. Abductor digiti minimi and flexor digiti minimi brevis attach to its base.
content.function: It forms the little toe's joint at the ball of the foot, letting it bend up and grip the ground.
content.mnemonic: Proximal means closest to the foot. Even the little toe starts with this bone.
content.clinical: Walking into furniture in the dark often breaks this bone. That is why it is nicknamed the night-walker's fracture.
content.hint: Find the little toe bone closest to the ball of the foot.

questions.text: Which muscle attaches to the base of the little toe's first bone?
questions.explanation: Abductor digiti minimi runs along the outer edge of the foot and attaches to the base of the little toe's proximal phalanx.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. This is the soldier in the middle.
content.location: It is the middle bone of the second toe, between its first bone and its tip. The big toe has no middle bone.
content.description: A short bone, much shorter than the first toe bone, with a joint at each end.
content.function: It adds a second bending joint to the toe. A muscle in the sole, flexor digitorum brevis, attaches to the middle bones of the four small toes.
content.mnemonic: Middle means in the middle, and the big toe skips it.
content.clinical: In hammer toe, this bone is held bent down. A painful corn can form where the bent joint rubs on the shoe.
content.hint: Find the in-between bone of the second toe.

questions.text: Which muscle attaches to the middle bones of the four small toes?
questions.explanation: Flexor digitorum brevis, a muscle in the sole, attaches to the middle phalanges of toes two to five.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. This is the middle soldier of the third toe.
content.location: It is the middle bone of the third toe, between its first bone and its tip.
content.description: A short little bone with a joint at each end, like a bead on a string.
content.function: It helps the toe curl so you can grip the ground. A muscle in the sole, flexor digitorum brevis, attaches to its sides.
content.mnemonic: Middle means middle. Small toes have one, and the big toe goes without.
content.clinical: Small toe breaks are usually treated by taping the toe to its neighbour and wearing a stiff-soled shoe.
content.hint: Find the in-between bone of the third toe.

questions.text: Which two bones does the middle phalanx of the third toe meet?
options: Proximal and distal phalanges of the third toe
questions.explanation: A middle phalanx sits between the first bone and the tip bone of its own toe, with a joint at each end.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. This is the fourth toe's middle soldier.
content.location: It is the middle bone of the fourth toe, between its first bone and its tip.
content.description: A short bone, much shorter than the first toe bone, with a small joint at each end.
content.function: It gives the fourth toe a second bending joint. A muscle in the sole, flexor digitorum brevis, attaches to its sides.
content.mnemonic: Middle bone, middle place. The big toe is the only one without it.
content.clinical: In claw toe, the joints on both sides of this bone bend down while the joint at the ball of the foot bends up.
content.hint: Find the in-between bone of the fourth toe.

questions.text: Which toe does NOT have a middle phalanx?
questions.explanation: The big toe has only two bones, near and far. Each of the small toes has a middle bone too.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. This is the little toe's middle soldier.
content.location: It is the middle bone of the little toe, between its first bone and its tip.
content.description: A tiny, short bone with a joint at each end. In many people it is joined to the tip bone.
content.function: It adds a joint to the little toe, though that joint hardly moves.
content.mnemonic: Middle means middle. The big toe skips it, and the little toe often merges it with the tip.
content.clinical: In many people it is fused with the tip bone, so the little toe shows only two bones on an X-ray. That is normal, not an injury.
content.hint: Find the in-between bone of the little toe.

questions.text: Where is the middle phalanx of the little toe?
options: Between the fifth metatarsal and the cuboid
At the base of the big toe
Between the first and tip bones of the little toe
questions.explanation: The middle phalanx lies between the first bone and the tip bone of its toe.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. Hallux, the Latin name for the big toe, is where this bone lives.
content.location: It is the tip bone of the big toe, in front of its first bone.
content.description: A short, broad bone with a rough, flat tip that supports the toe pad and toenail.
content.function: It gives the big toe a firm tip for the final push-off in walking. Flexor hallucis longus bends it from underneath, and extensor hallucis longus straightens it from on top.
content.mnemonic: Distal is distant from the foot, right at the tip. Both long big toe muscles end here.
content.clinical: Ingrown toenails most often affect the big toe. Crushing the tip can break this bone and cause a painful bruise under the nail.
content.hint: Find the tip bone of the big toe, under the largest toenail.

questions.text: Which muscle attaches under the base of the big toe's tip bone?
questions.explanation: Flexor hallucis longus attaches under the base of the big toe's tip bone and bends the toe down.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. This is the front soldier of the second toe.
content.location: It is the tip bone of the second toe, under the toenail.
content.description: A tiny bone with a flat, rough tip that props up the toe pad and nail.
content.function: It supports the toe tip. Flexor digitorum longus bends it from below, and extensor digitorum longus lifts it from above.
content.mnemonic: Distal means distant from the foot. It is the toe tip.
content.clinical: Mallet toe is a fixed bend at the joint just behind this bone. The tip points down and can rub on the shoe.
content.hint: Find the tip bone of the second toe.

questions.text: Mallet toe is a fixed bend at which joint?
options: The joint just before the tip bone
The joint between metatarsal and first toe bone
The joint between talus and calcaneus
questions.explanation: In mallet toe, the last joint of the toe stays bent, so the tip bone points down.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. This is the third toe's front-line soldier.
content.location: It is the tip bone of the third toe, under the toenail.
content.description: A tiny bone with a flattened, rough tip, like a little shelf for the toe pad and nail.
content.function: It supports the toe tip and nail. The long muscle flexor digitorum longus pulls on it from below to curl the tip.
content.mnemonic: Distal is distant, so it is the toe tip.
content.clinical: Dropping something heavy on your foot can break toe tips like this one, sometimes with blood trapped under the nail.
content.hint: Find the tip bone of the third toe.

questions.text: Which long muscle bends the tips of the four small toes?
questions.explanation: Flexor digitorum longus attaches to the tip bones of toes two to five and curls them down.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. This is the fourth toe's soldier at the front.
content.location: It is the tip bone of the fourth toe, under the toenail.
content.description: A tiny bone with a flat, rough tip that supports the toe pad and nail.
content.function: It supports the toe tip and nail. Flexor digitorum longus attaches below, and extensor digitorum longus on top.
content.mnemonic: Distal means distant, so think of it as the bone at the far end.
content.clinical: Crushed toe tips can break this bone. They usually heal with protection and taping.
content.hint: Find the tip bone of the fourth toe.

questions.text: Where is the distal phalanx of the fourth toe?
options: At the base of the fourth toe
At the tip of the fourth toe
Under the head of the fourth metatarsal
questions.explanation: Distal phalanges are the tip bones of the toes, sitting under the nails.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. This is the little toe's last soldier.
content.location: It is the tip bone of the little toe, under the toenail.
content.description: A tiny bone with a flat, rough tip that props up the toe pad and nail.
content.function: It supports the tip and nail of the little toe. Flexor digitorum longus pulls on it from underneath.
content.mnemonic: Distal is distant, at the tip. On the little toe it often teams up with the middle bone.
content.clinical: In many people this bone is fused with the middle bone. That is a normal variation, not an injury.
content.hint: Find the tip bone of the little toe.

questions.text: In many people, the tip bone of the little toe is fused with which bone?
options: Proximal phalanx of the little toe
Middle phalanx of the little toe
questions.explanation: In many people, the middle and tip bones of the little toe grow together. It is a common, normal variation.
